Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(InStyle.com) -- It takes a truly adventurous actress to pull off a razored Mohawk, a platinum pixie and a Louise Brooks bob, but we'd expect nothing less from the ever provocative Selma Blair, who experimented with all three looks in under a year. Selma Blair says she works with hairstylists and makeup artists who "have a vision." "I have no fears when it comes to my hair or clothes," proclaims the 36-year-old star of NBC's upcoming mom-and-daughter sitcom "Kath and Kim" and July's action flick "Hellboy II: The Golden Army." Makeup, however, is an entirely different matter for the self-declared "poor applier," who sticks with basics like nude lipstick and pink blush, and ducks whenever she sees a liquid liner. "I avoid anything difficult," she says. Blair's signature look: "A rosy cheek, a smudgy eye, a lot of mascara--I look like a doll that has too much makeup on, and I love it!" Have you always been a beauty chameleon? In high school I would mess with my hair and makeup all the time. I used to wear a shirt that said "Ms. Clairol" because I changed my hair color so much. I was blond for a long time, then what my mom called "barnyard red." Do you still dye it yourself? Only when I have to cover up stray grays. And I'll just use whatever color I find in the grocery store that looks good on the box, like Preference by L'Oréal--because I'm worth it [laughs]. But for my platinum hair, I went to Sheri at Román Salon in L.A. She was a saint. I had just dyed my hair dark brown, so she had to very slowly strip out all the color so that my hair wouldn't burn off. And the cut--are you keeping it short? I tend to like my hair whatever way it's not, so now I miss it being long. I think I'm more approachable with long hair. When it's short, I come across as being artsy and weird. What's your typical makeup look? I used to wear a lot of red lipstick, and when I got a pimple, I'd cover it up with eyeliner to turn it into a beauty mark. But everything has changed since I hit 35. I'm at an age where any makeup that's meant to look "slept in" really looks like I slept in it. That's for youngsters! Now less is more. I don't like to wear concealer or anything. I'd rather have uneven skin than feel like my face is cracking from too much foundation. Then you must be serious about your skin care. I go to a spa in L.A. called Kinara for its Skin Care BootCamp. You go once a week for 12 sessions and they'll look at your skin and tell you how to get it in better condition. They really helped me a lot. I also stay out of the sun. Any thoughts on Botox or plastic surgery? I wanted to get Botox once to make me feel younger. But I don't really have [enough wrinkles] to justify it yet. As for going under the knife, I can't say I wouldn't, but I haven't thought too much about it. Best beauty product? Egyptian Magic cream is my saving grace for everything. It works for my friend's baby's bottom, and I can also use it instead of Chapstick. So what's next? I'm really excited about having a perma-tan and wearing long highlighted hair extensions for my role on "Kath and Kim." And I've been gaining weight for the part by eating a little bit more of what I want and not moving around as much. I've already put on 15 pounds, and I'll probably gain another 10. It'll be a whole new me! Will this be your most drastic transformation? Actually I wore huge prosthetic boobs for a John Waters movie. They were glued on every day by a really handsome guy, but ripping them off every night was definitely outside my realm of comfort. After those bosoms, I didn't mind being flat-chested anymore! outputs.L1:
(InStyle.com) — It takes a truly adventurous actress to carry off a razored Mohawk, a platinum pixie, and a Louise Brooks bob—but we would expect nothing less from the ever-provocative Selma Blair, who tried all three looks in less than a year.

Blair says she works with hairstylists and makeup artists who “have a vision.”

“I have no fears when it comes to my hair or clothes,” declares the 36-year-old star of NBC’s upcoming mother-daughter sitcom *Kath and Kim* and July’s action film *Hellboy II: The Golden Army*.

Makeup, however, is another matter entirely for the self-described “poor applier,” who sticks to basics such as nude lipstick and pink blush—and ducks whenever she sees liquid liner.

“I avoid anything difficult,” she says.

Blair’s signature look? “A rosy cheek, a smudgy eye, a lot of mascara—I look like a doll that has too much makeup on, and I love it!”

**Have you always been a beauty chameleon?**  
In high school, I was always experimenting with my hair and makeup. I used to wear a shirt that said “Ms. Clairol” because I changed my hair color so often. I was blond for a long time, and then what my mother called “barnyard red.”

**Do you still dye it yourself?**  
Only when I need to cover up stray grays. I’ll just use whatever color I find at the grocery store that looks good on the box, like Preference by L’Oréal—because I’m worth it [laughs]. But for my platinum hair, I went to Sheri at Román Salon in L.A. She was a saint. I had just dyed my hair dark brown, so she had to strip out all the color very slowly so my hair wouldn’t burn off.

**And the cut—are you keeping it short?**  
I tend to like my hair whatever way it isn’t, so now I miss having it long. I think I’m more approachable with long hair. When it’s short, I come across as artsy and weird.

**What is your typical makeup look?**  
I used to wear a lot of red lipstick, and when I got a pimple, I’d cover it with eyeliner and turn it into a beauty mark. But everything has changed since I turned 35. I’m at an age where any makeup meant to look “slept in” really looks like I slept in it. That’s for youngsters! Now, less is more. I don’t like to wear concealer or anything. I’d rather have uneven skin than feel as though my face is cracking from too much foundation.

**Then you must be serious about skin care.**  
I go to a spa in L.A. called Kinara for its Skin Care BootCamp. You go once a week for 12 sessions, and they look at your skin and tell you how to get it into better condition. They really helped me a lot. I also stay out of the sun.

**Any thoughts on Botox or plastic surgery?**  
I wanted to get Botox once to make myself feel younger, but I don’t really have [enough wrinkles] to justify it yet. As for going under the knife, I can’t say I wouldn’t, but I haven’t thought too much about it.

**Best beauty product?**  
Egyptian Magic cream is my saving grace for everything. It works for my friend’s baby’s bottom, and I can also use it instead of Chapstick.

**So what’s next?**  
I’m really excited about having a perma-tan and wearing long, highlighted hair extensions for my role on *Kath and Kim*. And I’ve been gaining weight for the part by eating a little more of what I want and not moving around as much. I’ve already put on 15 pounds, and I’ll probably gain another 10. It’ll be a whole new me!

**Will this be your most drastic transformation?**  
Actually, I wore huge prosthetic breasts for a John Waters movie. They were glued on every day by a really handsome guy, but ripping them off every night was definitely outside my realm of comfort. After those bosoms, I didn’t mind being flat-chested anymore!

(InStyle.com) — Not many actresses are daring enough to convincingly wear a razor-cut Mohawk, a pale-blond pixie cut, and a Louise Brooks-style bob, but Selma Blair has never been one to play it safe. In less than a year, the famously bold performer tried all three hairstyles.

Blair says she likes collaborating with hair and makeup professionals who “have a vision.” The 36-year-old actress, who stars in NBC’s forthcoming mother-daughter sitcom *Kath and Kim* and appears in July’s action film *Hellboy II: The Golden Army*, says, “I have no fears when it comes to my hair or clothes.”

Cosmetics are another story. Blair describes herself as a “poor applier” and keeps her routine simple, relying on items such as nude lipstick and pink blush. Liquid eyeliner, she admits, is something she avoids. “I avoid anything difficult,” she says.

Her go-to beauty style? “A rosy cheek, a smudgy eye, a lot of mascara—I look like a doll that has too much makeup on, and I love it!”

**Have you always changed up your beauty look so often?**  
When I was in high school, I was constantly experimenting with both my hair and makeup. I even had a shirt that said “Ms. Clairol” because I switched hair colors so frequently. For quite a while I was blond, and then I had a shade my mother referred to as “barnyard red.”

**Do you still color your hair at home?**  
Only if I need to hide a few random gray hairs. I’ll just pick up whatever dye at the supermarket looks appealing on the box, like Preference by L’Oréal—because I’m worth it [laughs]. But when I went platinum, I saw Sheri at Román Salon in Los Angeles. She was amazing. I had just colored my hair dark brown, so she had to remove the color very gradually to keep my hair from burning off.

**What about the cut—will you keep it short?**  
I usually want my hair to be the opposite of whatever it currently is, so now I miss having long hair. I think I seem more approachable with longer hair. With short hair, I feel like I come off as artsy and strange.

**What is your everyday makeup style like?**  
I used to wear a lot of red lipstick, and if I got a pimple, I would disguise it with eyeliner and make it look like a beauty mark. But everything shifted once I turned 35. At this age, makeup that is supposed to look “slept in” just looks like I actually slept in it. That’s for younger people! Now I believe less is better. I don’t like wearing concealer or much of anything. I’d rather have uneven skin than feel as though my face is cracking under too much foundation.

**So you must take skin care seriously.**  
I go to Kinara, a spa in Los Angeles, for its Skin Care BootCamp. You attend once a week for 12 sessions, and they examine your skin and advise you on how to improve it. It helped me enormously. I also avoid the sun.

**What do you think about Botox or cosmetic surgery?**  
At one point I wanted Botox because I thought it might make me feel younger. But I don’t really have enough wrinkles yet to warrant it. As for surgery, I won’t say I’d never do it, but I haven’t spent much time thinking about it.

**What is your favorite beauty product?**  
Egyptian Magic cream is my lifesaver for everything. It works on my friend’s baby’s bottom, and I can use it in place of Chapstick, too.

**What transformation is coming next?**  
I’m very excited to have a permanent-looking tan and wear long highlighted hair extensions for my role on *Kath and Kim*. I’ve also been gaining weight for the character by eating a bit more of what I want and not moving as much. I’ve already gained 15 pounds, and I’ll probably add another 10. It’ll be an entirely new version of me!

**Will that be your biggest change yet?**  
Actually, I once had to wear enormous prosthetic breasts for a John Waters film. A very handsome man glued them onto me every day, but having them torn off each night was definitely beyond my comfort zone. After dealing with those breasts, I stopped minding being flat-chested!

outputs.L3:
Selma Blair has long been known for her willingness to take risks with her appearance, especially when it comes to dramatic hairstyles. Over the years, she has experimented with striking looks such as a razored Mohawk, a platinum pixie cut, and a sleek Louise Brooks-inspired bob. Rather than playing it safe, Blair has embraced transformation as part of her personal style.

Blair has said that she has no fear when it comes to hair or clothing. She enjoys bold choices and is drawn to creative collaborators who know exactly what they want to do. In particular, she prefers working with stylists and makeup artists who have a strong vision, trusting them to help create memorable looks rather than simply following conventional beauty rules.

Although she is adventurous with her hair and fashion, Blair has admitted that makeup is not her strongest skill. She considers herself poor at applying it and tends to rely on simple, familiar basics. Her usual routine includes nude lipstick, pink blush, mascara, and smudgy eyes—an understated approach compared with the more daring changes she makes to her hair and wardrobe.

Her interest in changing her hair goes back many years. Blair has been experimenting with hair color since high school, and even now she sometimes dyes it herself, particularly when she wants to cover gray hairs. This long history of coloring and restyling reflects her ongoing comfort with reinvention.

Still, Blair has acknowledged that her feelings about her hair are constantly shifting. She often finds herself wanting the opposite of whatever style she currently has. When her hair is short, she may long for it to be longer, and when it is long, she may feel tempted to cut it again. She has also observed that long hair can make her seem more approachable, while short hair creates a sharper, more dramatic impression. Through all of these changes, Blair’s style remains defined by confidence, experimentation, and a fearless attitude toward beauty.

Selma Blair has never been one to treat beauty as something fixed or predictable. Over the years, she has embraced hair and fashion as forms of self-expression, using them to shift moods, create characters, and surprise people. Rather than settling into one signature look, she seems to enjoy transformation itself—the thrill of cutting, coloring, styling, and reinventing.

Her approach to hair, in particular, has been fearless. Blair has moved confidently from a dramatic Mohawk to a striking platinum pixie, and later to a sleek bob, proving that she is comfortable taking risks most people would hesitate to try. Each change has felt less like a random experiment and more like another chapter in her evolving personal style. Whether edgy, polished, punk-inspired, or classic, her hair has often reflected a willingness to play with image and expectation.

Fashion appears to occupy a similar space for her. Blair is drawn to looks that make a statement, and she has often favored clothing with personality—pieces that feel bold, slightly provocative, or unexpected. Her style suggests someone who understands the theatrical side of dressing and is unafraid to use fashion to project confidence, humor, or defiance. She does not seem interested in looking merely pretty or safe; instead, she often chooses looks that create a strong impression.

By contrast, her makeup routine is simpler and more cautious. While she may be daring with a haircut or an outfit, she tends to keep her face more understated. This balance makes her overall style feel more intentional: the drama is often in the silhouette, the color, the cut, or the attitude, while the makeup remains a quieter supporting element. Rather than competing with her hair and clothes, it allows them to take center stage.

This contrast is part of what makes Blair such a compelling beauty figure. She is a chameleon, but not in a way that feels calculated or artificial. Her transformations feel playful, instinctive, and personal. She understands that beauty can be fluid, and she seems to enjoy the freedom that comes with not being tied to one image.

From her daring haircuts to her adventurous fashion choices, Selma Blair has built a reputation as someone willing to experiment and push boundaries. Her evolving looks reinforce the public image that has long surrounded her: that of an actress with edge, wit, and a provocative sense of style. She remains memorable not because she follows trends, but because she makes change itself part of her identity.
